# Puggalakathā (Kv 1.1)

**ID:** Kv 1.1
**Section:** Kathāvatthu (kv)
**Collection:** Abhidhamma
**Title (Pali):** Puggalakathā
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/abh03m3.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Puggalakathā* ("Discourse on the Person") is the opening debate and primary doctrinal section of the *Kathāvatthu*, the fifth book of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka [Norman 1983]. It is devoted to refuting the belief in a substantial, permanent individual (*puggala*), defending the central Buddhist teaching of non-self (*anattā*) against the views of the Pudgalavādins [Norman 1983; Watanabe 1983]. According to analyses of early Buddhist dialectics, the discourse displays a highly formalized logical structure: it comprises nineteen sections structured around refutations (*niggaha*), which in turn deploy pentads (*pañcaka*)—such as the affirmative pentad (*anulomapañcaka*)—and tetrads (*catukka*), such as the rejoinder tetrad (*paṭikammacatukka*) [Watanabe 1983]. The treatise examines whether the "person" can be known as a real, ultimate fact alongside analytical categories such as the aggregates (*khandha*), sense spheres (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and faculties (*indriya*), and also engages the "undeclared questions" [Williams, Buddhism].

Scholars consider the *Puggalakathā* to form part of the oldest core of the *Kathāvatthu*, originating in a period of intense three-way doctrinal debate between the Vibhajyavādins, the Sarvāstivādins, and the Pudgalavādins [Skorupski 1991; Ronkin, Early Buddhist Metaphysics; Williams, Buddhism]. Although Theravāda tradition attributes the text to Moggaliputta Tissa during the reign of King Aśoka, this early core can plausibly be dated to the third or second century BCE [Skorupski 1991; Norman 1983]. A closely comparable refutation of the *pudgala* is preserved in the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma treatise *Vijñānakāya* [Skorupski 1991; Watanabe 1983].

Cross-linguistically, DharmaNexus aligns passages of the text with Sanskrit and Tibetan treatments of the person, notably chapter 9 of Vasubandhu's *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the *Dharmaskandha*, Sthiramati's *Pañcaskandhakavibhāṣā*, and the Tibetan *Karmaprajñapti* [DharmaNexus].
